meta.premise: Acadie is a people before it is a place: no Acadian province has ever existed, and the Acadians of 1755 lived in what are now Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. This pack asks where an Acadian province would be if the three Maritime provinces were redrawn on language alone. It takes their 2021 census cells as one scope, bisects them on the share of French mother tongue, and lets refinement move the line while every region stays in one piece, with no population target. The francophone side is named Acadie and the rest the Maritimes. Contiguity is hard, so Acadie is one piece: northern and eastern New Brunswick, from Madawaska and Restigouche to the Acadian Peninsula, Kent and Moncton–Dieppe, with the thinly peopled interior that joins them, and one cell of Prince Edward Island's Évangéline region, at Wellington, joined across the Northumberland Strait by one of the mesh's sea crossings. The rest of Évangéline and the Acadian communities of Nova Scotia (Clare, Argyle, Chéticamp, Isle Madame) are too small and too far away to join it, and stay in the Maritimes. French is measured as mother tongue, not identity or ancestry, so the line is where French is the language people first learned, as the 2021 census counted it, not where Acadians live or lived.

federalism.title: Senate divisions
federalism.citation: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 22 (four divisions of 24 senators, with Newfoundland and the territories added)
federalism.detail: The Senate is built from four equal divisions of provinces. A region that spans two divisions has no seat count that follows from the text. No region spans two Senate divisions.

federalism.title: The 7/50 amending formula
federalism.citation: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 38(1) (resolutions of two-thirds of the provinces with at least half the population)
federalism.detail: Two-thirds of the units, holding at least half the population, can amend the constitution. With a different number of units, the threshold is a different set of people. Two-thirds of 2 units is 2. The 2 largest hold 100% of the people; the 2 smallest hold 100%. Any 2 units can amend alone.

federalism.title: Equalization
federalism.citation: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 36(2) (equalization payments so provinces can provide reasonably comparable services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation)
federalism.detail: Equalization measures fiscal capacity per person against the national average. Redrawing the units moves the average and changes who is below it. 1 of 2 regions fall below the set's GDP per person; Acadie is furthest below it. GDP here is an allocation, so read this as a shape, not a payment.

federalism.title: Quebec's asymmetry
federalism.citation: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 94, 133 and Constitution Act, 1982, s. 59 (Quebec's civil law, its legislature and its language guarantees)
federalism.detail: Quebec's civil law, language guarantees and opt-outs attach to Quebec as a unit. A set that cuts Quebec into pieces has to say which piece they attach to. This scope does not include Quebec.

federalism.title: Territorial status
federalism.citation: Northwest Territories Act, S.C. 2014, c. 2, s. 2; Yukon Act, S.C. 2002, c. 7; Nunavut Act, S.C. 1993, c. 28 (territories are created by Parliament, not by the constitutional amending formula)
federalism.detail: The territories exist by federal statute and can be changed by Parliament alone; provinces cannot. A region joining territory to province mixes the two. This scope has no territory in it.

federalism.title: The senatorial floor on Commons seats
federalism.citation: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 51A (no province has fewer Commons seats than senators)
federalism.detail: The floor keeps small provinces over-represented in the Commons. It is written for provinces as they are; new units of very different size change who it protects. The smallest region holds 14.9% of the set's people.
